newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S.Australia eyes petroleum retention licences.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S.Australia eyes petroleum retention licences.

text.p: The South Australian state government is considering introducing petroleum retention licences (PRL) which would give oil and gas producer Santos Ltd security over currently non-commercial discoveries in the onshore Cooper Basin beyond 1999.
Petroleum Exploration Licences (PEL) 5 and 6 held by Santos over 73,000 square km in and around the Cooper Basin in South Australia are due to expire in February 1999.
South Australian Mines and Energy Minister Stephen Baker said Santos had embarked on an ambitious A$200 million exploration programme in the lease areas leading up to the expiration date.
"To embark upon that programme they obviously wanted some level of comfort that they would not be drilling for somebody else in the process," he told Reuters in a recent interview.

"There are discussions taking place on the basis of possible retention licences for certain parts of the area but obviously we want to open it up as much as possible for competitive drilling," he said.

Santos originally held exploration leases covering half a million square km in South Australia, which over time have been reduced to PELs 5 and 6, granted to Santos and Delhi Petroleum Pty Ltd in 1979 to replace pre-existing licences.
Since 1954 Santos has discovered 119 gas fields and 55 oil fields in the region, and currently holds 70 production licences over 3400 square km in the PELs area.

According to a recent publication, the Mines Department's January 1993 estimate for the Cooper Basin of remaining gas potential was 1,260 petajoules of sales gas occurring in 204 fields and of 18.2 million barrels of oil in 122 new fields assuming gas exploration carries most of the risk of dry wells.

The department said the government plans to divide those areas of PELs 5 and 6 not under retention or production licences in 1999 into 2000-5000 square km lots, depending on their perceived prospectivity, and to open them to bids.

PRLs, which are available for mineral explorers in South Australia and petroleum explorers in other states, apply to finds which for generally technical or economic reasons are not immediately economic viable but hold some future potential.
"Certainly there are some discoveries we have made in the Cooper Basin which would be of that category," Santos executive general manager, commercial, John McArdle told Reuters.
"So when and if the government introduces retention licences we will be applying for some," he said.

McArdle said he would be surprised if there was opposition to the plan from other explorers seeking access to the Cooper Basin beyond 1999, saying retention licences were accepted by most people as a standard part of the exploration industry.
"If they are disappointed about retention licences being issued, then what they are saying is they want a free ride, they want to get hold of someone else's discovery," he said.
McArdle said Santos would be eligible to bid for the freed-up exploration leases in 1999, and would do so depending on its assessment of prospectivity and cost at that time.

He said Santos was also holding continuing talks with the state Mines and Energy Department over possible access to the Cooper Basin joint venture facilities, including the Moomba processing plant, for other potential producers there.

However he said while the state government would no doubt like certainty in the lead-up to the lease offerings, Santos considered the issue hypothetical because currently the plant was fully utilised and would be for the next decade at least.

"If for some reason we do not need it ... then of course we will talk to anyone who wants to use it ... it is certainly putting the cart before the horse to talk about access maybe 20 years in advance of when it actually might happen," he said.
